title: Test repositories never run Git background maintenance, so a test cannot fail while it removes its own repository
public_title: Stop Git background maintenance from breaking test cleanup
acceptance: Why. With Git 2.55 (the version the Linux CI runner installs from the git-core PPA), every `git commit` starts `git maintenance run --auto --quiet --detach` in the background and returns before that process ends. Right after the commit, that process can still hold `.git/objects/maintenance.lock`. When a test removes its repository in that moment, the removal fails with `Directory not empty: 'objects'`. This failed `tests/review-verdict.test.sh` on pull request #256 (run 38047822331), and a similar race broke a repository copy in a test of pull request #266. Each such red run costs a rerun and a diagnosis.

Evidence. firstmate ran a docker experiment on ubuntu:24.04 with Git 2.55.0 from the git-core PPA: a repository like the test fixtures, one commit, then a check for `.git/objects/maintenance.lock` right after the commit returned. With default settings the lock was there in 19 of 60 runs with half a CPU, and in 71 of 150 runs under heavy CPU load. With `maintenance.autoDetach=false`, or with `maintenance.auto=false`, it was there in 0 of 60 runs. Git 2.47 added `maintenance.autoDetach` (it falls back to `gc.autoDetach`, default true); before 2.47, automatic maintenance ran in the foreground, as it does with Git 2.45 on the operator's Mac. The record is a local firstmate note and is not in the repository; the pull request repeats these numbers and the Git version.

Why one place does not work. 15 test files under `tests/` remove every `GIT_*` variable from the environment they give to child processes, and 20 test files set `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, most of them together with `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`. A global or system Git config file, or `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, does not reach the repositories those tests create. `PATH` does: the tests keep it and only put their own tool folders in front of it.

How, the shared helper. `bin/fm-config.sh` gets one function, `fm_git_quiet <folder>`. On Linux (`uname -s` prints `Linux`) it finds the real `git` on the current `PATH`, writes an executable file `<folder>/git` that runs `exec <real git path> -c maintenance.autoDetach=false "$@"`, and puts `<folder>` first on `PATH` with `export`. On any other system it changes nothing and returns 0. A setting given with `-c` on the command line wins over every Git config file, and it is not removed when a test removes the `GIT_*` variables. When the first `git` on `PATH` is already such a wrapper (for example, `bin/ci.sh` started from a workflow step that already called `fm_git_quiet`), `fm_git_quiet` wraps it again. The result is the same setting given twice, which is allowed and harmless. With this setting, automatic maintenance still runs, but in the foreground: the Git command returns only after it ends, as before Git 2.47 and on the operator's Mac (captain, 2026-10-10).

How, the callers. There are four callers. (1) `bin/ci.sh` calls `fm_git_quiet "$ci_tmp/git-quiet"` once, right after it creates `ci_tmp` (about line 345) and before any stage starts. So the wrapper reaches every stage `bin/ci.sh` runs: the fast stage (shellcheck and the lints), the bash suites, the bun tests, the voyage node tests and the playwright tests. (2) `bin/fm-failfirst.sh` calls `fm_git_quiet "$work/git-quiet"` right after it creates `work` (about line 130). That script runs changed suites itself in the separate fail-first CI job (`.github/workflows/ci.yml` about lines 626-629, the `xargs ... bash "$work/one.sh"` call at about line 567), not through `bin/ci.sh`. A fail-first check shows that a test fails on the old code and passes on the new code; the fail-first CI job runs the suites a pull request changes on both versions. (3) and (4) In `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the bash job (about lines 282-283) and the fail-first job (about lines 623-624) each run `bash tests/pinned-context.test.sh` and `bash tests/review-experiment-evidence.test.sh` directly, before `bin/ci.sh` or `bin/fm-failfirst.sh` starts. Both suites create Git repositories. In each of those two steps, before the two suites, add `. bin/fm-config.sh && fm_git_quiet "$RUNNER_TEMP/git-quiet"`, so the two suites run with the wrapper first on `PATH`.

macOS. On macOS, `bin/ci.sh` and `bin/fm-failfirst.sh` behave exactly as today, because `fm_git_quiet` changes nothing there. This keeps the local pre-push run of `bin/ci.sh` and the macOS round sandbox (which checks whether the first `git` on `PATH` is an Apple xcrun shim) unchanged. A round is one worker or reviewer run on a task.

For `bin/ci.sh` and `bin/fm-failfirst.sh`, the wrapper folder lives under the temporary folder of the script that made it, so it is removed when that script exits, and only that script and its child processes see the changed `PATH`. In the two workflow steps, the changed `PATH` lasts until the step's shell exits (each step starts a new shell), and the runner discards `$RUNNER_TEMP` when the job ends. Other programs, such as the rounds firstmate starts and the board (the web page where the captain answers cards), keep the `PATH` they had.
When `fm_git_quiet` runs on Linux and finds no `git` on `PATH`, it prints `fm_git_quiet: git not found on PATH` to standard error and returns 70.

`bin/ci.sh` stops with exit code 70 when `fm_git_quiet` returns nonzero, instead of running without the wrapper. `bin/fm-failfirst.sh` needs no new stop for a missing `git`: it already exits 70 with "not inside a git checkout" (about line 124), before it reaches the call.
The wrapper prints nothing of its own. Arguments, standard input, standard output, standard error and the exit code are those of the real `git`, because the wrapper uses `exec`.

Test reach. Add `tests/ci-git-wrapper.test.sh`. It builds a fixture tree the way `tests/ci-lints.test.sh` (about lines 11-19) does: it copies `bin/ci.sh`, `bin/fm-config.sh` and the config modules into the fixture, adds one probe suite `tests/probe.test.sh`, and runs `FM_TEST_OS=Linux PATH="<uname shim>:$PATH" FM_ROOT=<fixture> bash <fixture>/bin/ci.sh --stage bash`, with the `uname` shim from `tests/ci-budget.test.sh` (about line 158). The probe suite creates a repository with every `GIT_*` variable removed except `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null` and `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`, and writes what it sees to a file the test then reads. It calls `fm_git_quiet` directly only for the assertions `linux: missing git stops` and `macOS: nothing changes`. The assertion `fail-first job: suites run with the wrapper` runs `bin/fm-failfirst.sh`, and `linux ci: missing git stops bin/ci.sh` runs the fixture `bin/ci.sh`.
Fail-first assertion `linux ci: maintenance.autoDetach is false`: in the probe repository, `git config --get maintenance.autoDetach` prints `false`.

Regression assertion `linux ci: automatic maintenance is not turned off`: in the probe repository, `git config --get maintenance.auto` prints nothing and `git config --get gc.auto` prints nothing, so the wrapper adds no other setting.

Regression assertion `linux ci: no maintenance outlives a commit`: right after a `git commit` in the probe repository returns, no process whose arguments start with `git maintenance` is running for that repository, and `.git/objects/maintenance.lock` does not exist. On Git before 2.47 this holds on base too, so it is a regression check, not a fail-first one.

Fail-first assertion `fail-first job: suites run with the wrapper`: the test builds a fixture repository the way `tests/failfirst.test.sh` does (its `fixture` function, about lines 15-30: a `main` commit and a `change` branch, with a `config.yaml` whose `test` template is `case {file} in *.test.sh) bash {file} ;; esac`). The change edits the behaviour file `bin/tool.sh` (as `tests/failfirst.test.sh` about lines 41-42 does), so the script has a change to revert, and adds `tests/probe.test.sh`. The probe creates a new repository with every `GIT_*` variable removed except `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null` and `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`, and appends the output of `git config --get maintenance.autoDetach` as one line to a file named by an environment variable. The test runs `( cd <fixture> && FM_TEST_OS=Linux PATH="<uname shim>:$PATH" bash <repo>/bin/fm-failfirst.sh main )` and requires the file to hold exactly two lines (one from the run on the head and one from the run on the base), both `false`. If the call in `bin/fm-failfirst.sh` is removed, both lines are empty and the assertion fails.
Fail-first assertion `linux: missing git stops`: with a `PATH` built by `fixture_path <dir> 'git'` (`tests/lib/path.sh`), `fm_git_quiet` prints `fm_git_quiet: git not found on PATH` and returns 70.

Fail-first assertion `linux ci: missing git stops bin/ci.sh`: the fixture `bin/ci.sh --stage bash`, run with `FM_TEST_OS=Linux` and a `PATH` built by `fixture_path <dir> 'git'` plus the `uname` shim, exits 70 and prints `fm_git_quiet: git not found on PATH`.
Fail-first assertion `macOS: nothing changes`: with `FM_TEST_OS=Darwin` and the `uname` shim, `fm_git_quiet` returns 0, writes no file into the folder and leaves `PATH` unchanged.

Regression assertion `wrapper: arguments pass through`: through the wrapper, `git -c core.abbrev=12 rev-parse --short HEAD` in the probe repository prints the same text as the real `git` with the same arguments, and an argument with a space reaches Git unchanged (`git commit -qm 'two words'` stores the subject `two words`).
Regression assertion `wrapper: exit code passes through`: `git rev-parse --verify no-such-ref` exits with the same nonzero code through the wrapper as with the real `git`.
Regression assertion `wrapper: standard input passes through`: `printf x | git hash-object --stdin` prints the same object id through the wrapper as with the real `git`.

Fail-first assertion `workflow: direct suites use the wrapper`: in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, each step that runs `bash tests/pinned-context.test.sh` also runs `fm_git_quiet` earlier in the same step. The test reads the workflow file and checks this for every such step (two today), so a new direct step without the wrapper fails it.

intent.text: On Linux CI, every Git call runs its automatic maintenance in the foreground.
The fail-first job and the two workflow steps that run suites directly use the same wrapper.
On macOS, the CI script and the fail-first script run Git exactly as today.

why.text: Git 2.55 on the CI runner starts a background job after each commit.
A test that deletes its folder during that job fails at random.

done.text: Intent 1: tests show a commit returns only after maintenance ends, and maintenance and gc stay on.
Intent 2: tests show the fail-first job and both workflow steps use the wrapper.
Intent 3: a test shows nothing changes on macOS.

notes.text: The experiment proved the late Git job but did not catch the delete error itself.
